# Introduction
We follow [ISLR (2013)](#r1) pages 48 to 51 for loading data using `tidyverse` concepts.

# Packages
As usual, we have some standard packages. 
```{r}
library(ISLR2) # some data files
library(mbadtools)
```

# Data
The `Auto` dataset is in the `ISLR2` package. We discuss reading Excel and csv files in other notebooks.
```{r}
data(Auto)
```

Display the data by yelling its name.
```{r}
Auto
```

Summarize data easily:

```{r}
Auto %>% skim
```

There is no missing data in this dataset. but if some entries were missing, we could remove those rows with the `na.omit` function.

Column names can be retrieved like this:

```{r}
colnames(Auto)
```


# Graphical and Numeric Summaries

Scatterplots are easily done with `ggplot`. *We no longer use the `attach` function as it always led to trouble.*

```{r}
Auto %>% ggplot() + 
  geom_point(aes(cylinders, mpg))
```
Boxplots are also easy for categorical variables like `cylinders`. The `labs()` function adds titles, subtitles, x and y axis labels.
```{r}
Auto %>% ggplot() +
  geom_boxplot(aes(as.factor(cylinders), mpg), color="red") +
  labs(x="Cylinders",
       y="MPG")
```
# Histograms

In histograms I like to outline the bars in black, and make the fill the color I  want. I can use the alpha parameter to change the transparency. The info message can be suppressed by picking a bins number in the function, or simply using 'message=FALSE' in the {r}.
```{r message=FALSE}
Auto %>% ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(mpg), color="black", fill="red", alpha=0.5) +
  labs(x="MPG",
       y="Count")
```

# Pairs plot
The `ggplot` version also shows correlation coefficients and density plots. There are many options; see [GGally::ggpairs](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/GGally/topics/ggpairs).
```{r}
Auto %>% 
  select(mpg, displacement, horsepower, weight, acceleration) %>% 
  ggpairs(progress=F)
```

# Summary
The `summary` function still works and is quick, but the `skim` function is better. That's because you can actually grab the individual numbers out of the `skim` objects.

```{r}
Auto %>% summary()
Auto %>% skim()
```

From the `skim`, you can see that the `name` variable has 301 distinct character values, and there are no missing values in any of the 11 numeric variables.

If you want the median of `mpg` for instance, you can grab it from the `skim` output. Median is the 50th percentile.
```{r}
Auto %>% skim %>% select(skim_variable, numeric.p50) %>% 
  filter(skim_variable=="mpg")
```


# Conclusion
We found out how do things in sections 2.3.4 and 2.3.5 the modern tidyverse way.
